POORTER Palaeornaynetisch Laboratorium, Fort Hoofddijk, Rijksuniversiteit, Utrecht, The Netherlands Received 3 July 1971 Palaeomagnetic investigations were made on Precambrian rocks from Rogaland (southwestern Norway). Samples from anortho- site masses, a noritic layered intrusion and high grade metamor- phic migmatites, together called the basement, revealed a similar "reversed" magnetization. This is explained by a simultaneous magnetization during uplift after the Sveco-Norwegian regenera- tion. The pole position calculated for the basement rocks i

d 133 ° W. The age that can be assignated to this pole is 850-950×106 y. This is concluded from U/Pb I. Introduction The Rogaland Precambrian consists of high grade metamorphic migmatites enveloping anorthosite mas- ses and a lopolith-shaped noritic intrusion. The whole complex is dissected by dolerite dikes. The determina- tion of the pole-positions belonging to this complex seemed to be useful in establishing a palaeomagnetic stratigraphy for this part of the Baltic Shield, which might in turn enable us to correlate rock formations within this Shield. The Rogaland Precambrian in SW Norway has been the subject of geological and petrographical research of the department of petrography of the Utrecht State University since 1964. This research is directed by TOBI (1965). Previous geological investigations in this area were made by BARTH (1945), MICHOT (1957, 1960), ANTUN (1956), HEIER (1956), and BARTH and DONS (1960). Previous palaeomagnetic research in the Roga- land area has been carried out by STORETVEDT (1965) and STORETVEDT and GIDSKEHAUG (1968) on the Egersund dolerite dikes. 2. Discussion of the results The similar overall magnetic directions of the lopo- lith, the migmatite complex and the anorthosite masses, suggest a simultaneous magnetization. Hence, if the remanence is thermal in origin, a simultaneous cooling of these rock formations has to be assumed. The range of blocking temperatures, determined for the character- istic magnetizations, points to a temperature range of 550 to 650°C. This temperature range fits the tempera- tures involved in the amphibolite and granulite facies metamorphism of the migmatites. It is presumed that the characteristic magnetization originated during the cooling after this metamorphic event. The simultaneous cooling of the lopolith and the anorthosite masses together with the migmatites can be explained by a regional uplift. The variation in the direction of remanent magnetism with altitude has been studied. The palcomagnetic data reveal the occurrence of a reversal of the earth's magnetic field at ar altitude of about 975 meters at Amarkantak as well as the unstable behavior of the geomagnetic field near the polarity transition. These data are at variance with the observation of the same reversal of magnetic field at an altitude of about 625 meters in the palcomagnetic study of several other vertical sequenc'es in the Deccan traps. Gacii (Received 1970 January 22)t Summary Measurements on samples from 20 sites in the Ethiopian flood basalt succession yield a palaeomagnetic pole at 80.8" N, 167-7" E with a circle of confidence of 4.3". Szalay, Director of the Institute for Nuclear Research at Debrecen. A single specimen from each oriented core (sample) is measured and the unit Cretaceous, Tertiary and Quarternary palawmagnetic results 69 The measurement-demagnetization sequence gives a set of at least five directions for each core (independently oriented sample). A consecutive pair of these directions is taken for each core from the unit and the mean direction for the set is found. The procedure is then repeated for all possible combinations of pairs of directions to find which gives the least scatter. The corresponding mean direction is defined as the best direction for the unit. Least scatter is taken to give the largest value of the precision parameter, k = (N- l)/(N-R) (Fisher 1953) since this is readily calculated. (See for instance Irving 1964). With these facts in mind an objective method of choosing the best direction for each core as well for the unit as a whole is needed. When combined with measurements made on rocks from sites some 10 km away from ours, two paths con- necting these transitional virtual poles may be traced, one for the lower Pliocene and the other for the upper Pliocene. Both cross central Russia and the Indian Ocean. Palaeosecular variations of the geomagnetic field have been investigated by restricting our studies to flows which yield virtual poles at latitudes higher than 45" and the dispersion of cleaned R.M. directions obtained from such flows agree with world-wide average values. Thermomagnetic, ore microscope and electron microprobe investigations have been made and the shape of the thermomagnetic curves is related to evidence of both low and high temperature oxidation. 1. Introduction The volcanic rocks of Kyushu Island, Japan range in age from Miocene to Pleistocene (Table 1). Palaeomagnetic studies on them have previously been reported by Kawai er al. (1961, 1962) and also by Nomura (1967). The latter dis- covered some lava flows whose virtual geomagnetic poles computed after A.F. and thermal cleaning of the N.R.M., are situated in low latitudes and suggested that they record geomagnetic field directions during polarit

omagnetic poles lie in S.E. Australia (Figs 6 and 8). At fist we wondered whether an error of 180" had been made in the orientation of samples from these sites (we thought the wrong end of the compass needle might have been read). If this were so, these sites would belong to polarity class N. Creer and Y. ispir* (Received 1969 December 18)t Summary Some of these Cenozoic basalts are magnetized in either the normal or reversed direction of the axial dipole field but some others are magnetized obliquely. The remanences of the latter are quite as stable as the normal or reversed flows and are interpreted as recording geomagnetic field directions during polarity transitions. When combined with measurements made on rocks from sites some 10 km away from ours, two paths con- necting these transitional virtual poles may be traced, one for the lower Pliocene and the other for the upper Pliocene. Conclusion In the light of the variations observed in the Swett ignimbrite it is debatable how accurately these rocks reflect the geomagnetic field direction at the time of their deposition. But the directions of the Needles Range and Leach Canyon ignimbrites are clearly outside the range of any reasonable variations one might expect within a single flow. The possibility of remagnetization at a later time can be rejected since it could result in a direction only closer to the present pole. ‘Anomalous’ poles are fairly commonly observed in Tertiary rocks (e.g. Irving 1964, Gromm6 1965). Mort of these results are based on igneous rocks which cool below their Curie point in a very short time and thercfore represent spot readings. imbrites are in the rhyolite-dacite composition range and are welded to various degrees. The main minerals are quartz, sanidine, plagioclase, hornblende, and biotite but these rarely comprise more than 30 per cent of the rock, the remainder being glass. The lateral lithologic variation within units is usually small whereas the lithologic differences between units are great. The thicknesses range from 10 to about lo00 feet, the average being around 200 feet. The ages used in this paper are those reported by Armstrong (1969). Such a situation is generally met with in the case of igneous activities of uninterrupted nature. In this paper, the palaeomagnetic results on a suite of dolerite dykes, intrusive into Gondwana basins forming a part of the Damodar Valley coaliields of India have been reported, and the inferences based on these results regarding the interrelationship of four different Mesozoic volcanic activities in India are discussed. Geology and palaeomagnetism of the Mesozoic volcanics The Mesozoic volcanic activity in India is represented by four different outcrops of basaltic lavas (Fig. 1). s in fact, that the South Pole made a south-westward discursion during the late Permian towards the coincident Triassic polar regions of South America and Africa. All Permian formations studied so far from South America are reversely magnetized; the inclinations of the magnetic vectors are reversed with respect to the present geomagnetic field inclinations at the sampling sites. The Piaui formation is also reversely magnetized. The magnetizations are believed to date from the Kiaman Magnetic Interval which was first detected and defined from palaeomagnetic studies on Australian Upper Carboniferous and Permian formations (21), (22). A polarity change from ' normal ' to ' reversed ' was demonstrated by Irving (22), in the Upper Carboniferous section of Hunter Valley, New South Wales. Reversed geomagnetic polarity then persisted for almost the whole of the Permian period, the next major polarity change (to ' normal ') occurring in the Lower Triassic. The presence of the Kiaman Magnetic Interval in Permian formations of the U.S.A., the U.S.S.R. and western Europe has been indicated, and the possibility of inter-continental correlation has been discussed by McElhinny (23). Embleton (Received 1970 June 30) Summary Palaeomagnetic data are summarized for two collections of red-beds from the Middle Paganzo formation (Permian age) of La Rioja and San Juan Provinces, north-west Argentina. The thicker succession sampled in La Rioja allows us to trace the movement of the south palaeomagnetic pole which shifted during the Permian from 59.5" S, 2.5" W to 74" S, 52" W. The red-beds from San Juan yield a south palaeomagnetic pole situated at 63" S, 4" W. A basalt which occurs near the base of the La Colina formation (in the Paganzo type area, and directly equivalent to the middle Paganzo) yields a south virtual palaeomagnetic pole at 50" S, 3" E. The results are entirely consistent with previously published palaeomagnetic data for the Permian and Permo-Carboniferous of South America. 1. All Permian formations studied so far from South America are reversely magnetized; the inclinations of the magnetic vectors are reversed with respect to the present geomagnetic field inclinations at the sampling sites. The Piaui formation is also reversely magnetized. The magnetizations are believed to date from the Kiaman Magnetic Interval which was first detected and defined from palaeomagnetic studies on Australian Upper Carboniferous and Permian formations (21), (22). A polarity change from ' normal ' to ' reversed ' was demonstrated by Irving (22), in the Upper Carboniferous section of Hunter Valley, New South Wales. Reversed geomagnetic polarity then persisted for almost the whole of the Permian period, the next major polarity change (to ' normal ') occurring in the Lower Triassic. Embleton (Received 1970 June 30) Summary Palaeomagnetic data are summarized for two collections of red-beds from the Middle Paganzo formation (Permian age) of La Rioja and San Juan Provinces, north-west Argentina. The thicker succession sampled in La Rioja allows us to trace the movement of the south palaeomagnetic pole which shifted during the Permian from 59.5" S, 2.5" W to 74" S, 52" W. The red-beds from San Juan yield a south palaeomagnetic pole situated at 63" S, 4" W. A basalt which occurs near the base of the La Colina formation (in the Paganzo type area, and directly equivalent to the middle Paganzo) yields a south virtual palaeomagnetic pole at 50" S, 3" E. The results are entirely consistent with previously published palaeomagnetic data for the Permian and Permo-Carboniferous of South America. 1. Introduction Palaeomagnetic investigation of South American rock formations commenced in 1956. In 1958, K. M. Creer extended the work to north-west Argentina. of this pole position and its validity for the whole of the Permian period was desirable since the African and Australian palaeomagnetic data have been interpreted (5), (6) such that the palaeomagnetic record of South America appears to be incomplete. In fact, the similarity between the African and Australian data for the Upper Palaeozoic is striking (7), the resulting continental reconstruction supporting that of King's (8) earlier work. y of the Pikes Peak batholith The Pikes Peak batholith is oval shaped in outcrop and follows the axis of a regional north-south anticline formed in the highly metamorphosed Idaho Springs Formation (Fig. 1). On the eastern flanks the granite is overlain by several thousand feet of Upper Cambrian to Cretaceous deposits, many of these in fault contact with the granite (Boos & Boos 1957). Elsewhere it is overlain by sub-horizontal Tertiary sediments and volcanics, associated with Eocene intrusive stocks (Lovering & Goddard 1950). The composition of the batholith varies from older, outermost granodiorite to quartz monzonite to granite in fairly distinct shells (Hutchinson 1960). The texture is massively coarse grained and locally porphyritic. Contact metamorphic effects appear to be rare. Samples were obtained at 1-km intervals westwards along U.S. Highway 24 out of Colorado Springs. Unfortunately the proximity of the Ute Pass Fault may diminish the relevance of such a profile. The fault very roughly parallels the highway, and although it is a high-angle thrust, the granite is locally sheared and brecciated. In the laboratory, several cores 2.5 cm in diameter were drilled from each block sample, and specimens 2.5 cm long were cut from either end of each core. 5. Pilot demagnetization Two specimens from each sample were subjected to pilot demagnetization and the NRM measured on a PAR spinner magnetometer, Model SM-1, at the University of Texas at Dallas. The demagnetization equipment is located in a shielded mu- metal room (residual field < 200 y) and is described by Helsley & Spall (1970). One specimen was demagnetized in successive alternating fields (AF) of 88, 175, 350, 700 and 1400 Oe. There was little vector rotation during this operation. It is typically indicated by observations of a ' minimum intensity * during demagnetization, at which the NRM intensity fluctuates erratically, and the dispersion of directions between-specimens is high. Whatever its origin, the observation of a magnetization whose direction fluctuates greatly, suggests a useful limit to meaningful demagnetization. The second problem arose during thermal demagnetization. Some of the coarse- grained granites could not be heated more than once or twice above 500 "C, because they crumbled. Some of this extra complexity may be due to the exposed character of the sampling sites, most of which were natural outcrops on the tops of ridges. This contrasts with the Arrochar sites all of which were in quarries or streams at low topographic levels. THESIS The radiometric data imply a difference in age of no more than 70 m.y. between the alkali granite and the poststructure basic granophyre (Nicolaysen et al. 1963). If the alkali-granite masses were intruded after the overturning, their primary remanent magnetism should be similar to that of the basic granophyre, assuming restricted polar wander during this short interval. The declination deviates from that of %table” Northern Europe by about 50 O, but the inclination agrees well with the expected value. These devia- tions imply, in a general fashion, that large scale relative motions, either rotational or translational, have occurred between Tethys and its northern borderland. But much more data than is presently available is needed before these apparent motions can be evaluated quantitatively, This paper describes new observations (chiefly from Triassic igneous rocks) from the area of the Dolomites which is within the Tethys domain, and is intended as a contribution to this necessary body of knowledge. The Dolomites consist of little disturbed Permian and Mesozoic formations resting on a crystalline basement complex. There is no evidence of regional metamor- phism and nappe tectonics, and if large displacements have occurred they have almost certainly affected the region as a whole. It was for these reasons that this sampling region was chosen. ’ Present address: Laboratorio di Geologia Marina, Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, via Zamboni 67, Bologna (Italy). (Canada) (Received April 10, 1970) SUMMARY A paleomagnetic survey of Middle and Upper Triassic porphyrites, dykes, and tuffites from the Dolomites (Eastern Alps, Italy) has yielded an average direction (based on 57 samples from 12 collecting localities) with declination 329OE of true north and inclination +25O after magnetic cleaning and correction for geological dip. The declination deviates from that of %table” Northern Europe by about 50 O, but the inclination agrees well with the expected value. This indicates that the Dolomites area has rotated 50* anticlockwise relative to northern Europe since the Triassic but there is no evidence of relative changes in latitude. These devia- tions imply, in a general fashion, that large scale relative motions, either rotational or translational, have occurred between Tethys and its northern borderland. But much more data than is presently available is needed before these apparent motions can be evaluated quantitatively, This paper describes new observations (chiefly from Triassic igneous rocks) from the area of the Dolomites which is within the Tethys domain, and is intended as a contribution to this necessary body of knowledge. The Dolomites consist of little disturbed Permian and Mesozoic formations resting on a crystalline basement complex. There is no evidence of regional metamor- phism and nappe tectonics, and if large displacements have occurred they have almost certainly affected the region as a whole. It was for these reasons that this sampling region was chosen. ’ Present address: Laboratorio di Geologia Marina, Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, via Zamboni 67, Bologna (Italy). Both remanent magnetic polarity and the

Some of the Middle Keweena- wan volcanic units examined by Dubois (1962), exhibited reverse (positive) magnetic polarity, whereas other units consisted entirely of nor- mal (negative) polarity, but it was only for the Logan sills and dikes that Dubois (1962) had evidence suggesting the age relations be- tween these two sets of magnetic directions. The efforts of the present study were con- centrated on the volcanic sequences which are generally assigned to the Middle Keweenawan (Halls 1966, p. 5). Introduction The paleomagnetic survey of the Keweena- wan rocks in the Lake Superior region by Dubois ( 1962) illustrated the potential of the paleomagnetic method in supplementing radio- metric dating for the purpose of effecting stratigraphic correlations in unfossiliferous rocks. Both remanent magnetic polarity and the

f remanent magnetization were used to corre- late the various Keweenawan sequences around Lake Superior. Some of the Middle Keweena- wan volcanic units examined by Dubois (1962), exhibited reverse (positive) magnetic polarity, whereas other units consisted entirely of nor- mal (negative) polarity, but it was only for the Logan sills and dikes that Dubois (1962) had evidence suggesting the age relations be- tween these two sets of magnetic directions. The efforts of the present study were con- centrated on the volcanic sequences which are generally assigned to the Middle Keweenawan (Halls 1966, p. 5). Some of these have not been sampled by previous investigators, while others, such as that at Mamainse Point, have only been partly studied (Dubois 1962). Normal directions of magnetization, which differ from the reverse direc- tions of magnetization by amounts ranging from 140" to 163" occur throughout the Michipico- ten Island section, and in the upper p

nd Mamainse Point sections. Provided part of the section at Mamainse Point has been repeated by faulting, these new results, together with data from the literature, are compatible with a single polarity reversal in Middle Keweenawan time separating older reverse polarity rocks from stratigraph- ically younger normal polarity rocks. An estimate of the pole position during Middle Keweenawan time can, however, be made by calculating a pole given equal weight to the mean normal and mean reverse pole. This is calculated to be 159" W, 42" N. Introduction The paleomagnetic survey of the Keweena- wan rocks in the Lake Superior region by Dubois ( 1962) illustrated the potential of the paleomagnetic method in supplementing radio- metric dating for the purpose of effecting stratigraphic correlations in unfossiliferous rocks. Both remanent magnetic polarity and the

f remanent magnetization were used to corre- late the various Keweenawan sequences around Lake Superior. Some of the Middle Keweena- wan volcanic units examined by Dubois (1962), exhibited reverse (positive) magnetic polarity, whereas other units consisted entirely of nor- mal (negative) polarity, but it was only for the Logan sills and dikes that Dubois (1962) had evidence suggesting the age relations be- tween these two sets of magnetic directions. The efforts of the present study were con- centrated on the volcanic sequences which are generally assigned to the Middle Keweenawan (Halls 1966, p. 5). Some of these have not been sampled by previous investigators, while others, such as that at Mamainse Point, have only been partly studied (Dubois 1962). PALMER Department of Geophysics, The University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario Received April 13, 1970 Accepted for publication August 12, 1970 Paleomagnetic results from the Lake Superior region appear to indicate that Middle Keweenawan formations or magnetic divisions within formations can be correlated on the basis of magnetic polarity. The Logan sills, the volcanics of the Osler Group, the lava section at Alona Bay, the lower 6000 ft (1829 m) of North Shore volcanics, the lower 1000 ft (305 m) of Cape Gargantua volcanics and the lower 3000 ft (914 m) at Mamainse Point are of reverse polarity. Normal directions of magnetization, which differ from the reverse direc- tions of magnetization by amounts ranging from 140" to 163" occur throughout the Michipico- ten Island section, and in the upper p

nd Mamainse Point sections. Provided part of the section at Mamainse Point has been repeated by faulting, these new results, together with data from the literature, are compatible with a single polarity reversal in Middle Keweenawan time separating older reverse polarity rocks from stratigraph- ically younger normal polarity rocks. The mean direction of magnetization from a conglomer- ate test is defined with higher precision than would be expected from a randomly distributed population. It is believed that this mean direction reflects a secondary component of magnetiza- tion which cannot be preferentially removed by alternating field demagnetization and which has caused the non anti-parallel alignment of normal and reverse populations of magnetization. An estimate of the pole position during Middle Keweenawan time can, however, be made by calculating a pole given equal weight to the mean normal and mean reverse pole. This is calculated to be 159" W, 42" N. Introduction The paleomagnetic survey of the Keweena- wan rocks in the Lake Superior region by Dubois ( 1962) illustrated the potential of the paleomagnetic method in supplementing radio- metric dating for the purpose of effecting stratigraphic correlations in unfossiliferous rocks. Both remanent magnetic polarity and the

f remanent magnetization were used to corre- late the various Keweenawan sequences around Lake Superior. Some of the Middle Keweena- wan volcanic units examined by Dubois (1962), exhibited reverse (positive) magnetic polarity, whereas other units consisted entirely of nor- mal (negative) polarity, but it was only for the Logan sills and dikes that Dubois (1962) had evidence suggesting the age relations be- tween these two sets of magnetic directions. The efforts of the present study were con- centrated on the volcanic sequences which are generally assigned to the Middle Keweenawan (Halls 1966, p. 5). Some of these have not been sampled by previous investigators, while others, such as that at Mamainse Point, have only been partly studied (Dubois 1962). directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: Gif-sur-Yvette cedex, France b Estacion Volcanologica de Canarias, CSIC, La Laguna, Tenerife, Spain Received 6 June 1998; revised version received 20 November 1998; accepted 24 November 1998 Abstract We have sampled a sequence of 69 ¯ows in the island of El Hierro (Canary Islands). 46 of them belong to the El Golfo formation and 23 to the most recent rift formation. Radiometric dating brackets this section between 442 ka and 134 ka with six intermediate datings. All the samples were stepwise demagnetized, partly with alternative ®eld, partly thermally with very similar results. The large majority of the samples are characterized by a single stable component of magnetization. ChRM isolated after the ®rst steps of demagnetization are all of normal polarity. Inclinations are on average shallower than expected from a geocentered dipole ®eld, but consistent with results from other areas at the same latitude. Mean declinations of the rift and El Golfo sequences are both easterly deviated (about 5ë and 15ë respectively) and signi®cantly different suggesting that the section has undergone a progressive clockwise rotation. VGP scatter and directional scatter calculated for the rift sequence are consistent with available data from other geographical areas, and also with recent models of paleosecular vari

tle studied from a paleomag- netic point of view. Early studies [3±7] were aimed toward understanding of tectonic evolution of the is- lands, rather than documenting the paleosecular vari- ation. Discussion Eleven of the 14 sites sampled were con- sidered to have reliable mean-site remanence directions. The strike and dip of the diabase sheet at the 11 sites (Table I) were obtained from information compiled by Thomson ( 1960, pp. 18-20; 1961a, pp. 46-47; 1961b, pp. 17, 19, 22, 24, 52; 1961c, p. 43). All tectonic corrections were made by simple rotation of the dip plane to the horizontal about the strike. Applying the fold test (Graham 1949) to all 11 mean site remanence directions, the values of a95 before and after tectonic correction were 5.4' and 8.6" respectively. Snedecor's F-ratio test for the null hypothesis (Larochelle 1968) indicates that there is a probability of 0.97 that the scatter in the remanence directions caused by applying tectonic corrections is significant. These tests show that the diabase acquired its remanence after solidification of the primary basin and arch structure. There is some evidence that Thomson's (1957) suggestion that post-solidification tec- degrees. tonics accentuated the basin and arch structure is correct. The

post-solidification NW- SE contraction approximately perpendicular to the basin axis (N 50°E) and parallel to the major NW-SE fault set. Unfortunately 3 of the 4 sites (5, 6, 7, and 8) collected to define the limbs of the Kerr Lake Arch which might have provided useful additional data, are not reliable. Thus the data favor a minor amount of secondary folding but not on a statistical significance basis. Sites 9 and 10 are adjacent to the Beaver and Kerr Lake faults respectively where the diabase sheet dips at 60' and 15" respectively. Application of tectonic corrections causes the remanence directions to scatter from consistent primary directions to completely inconsistent directions. This result suggests that the diabase SYMONS: PAL was not folded by more than a very few de- grees adjacent to the major faults contrary to Knight's ( 1922) suggestion. Sites 11 to 14 are collected on a N-S traverse perpendicular to the E-W ore vein structures of the Silverfields mine where the diabase sheet is flat-lying (Moore 1967; Petruk 1968). If post-solidification tectonics caused the sheet to fracture into blocks defined by the veins, then the remanence directions might reflect some consistent deformation pattern. SYMONS Geological Survey of Canada, 601 Booth Street, Ottawa, Canada Received September 9, 1969 Accepted for publication November 12, 1969 At Cobalt the Nipissing diabase intrusive occurs as a 1000 ft (-305 m) thick undulating sheet exposed in a series of basin and arch structures from which 112 specimens were collected at 14 sites. Paleomag- netic analysis of the cleaned natural remanence directions from the 11 acceptable sites suggests that these structures are dominantly primary. Minor post-solidification compression associated with the NW-SE trending faults may have amplified the primary NE-SW axial trends of the structures. Significant folding adjacent to the faults does not appear probable. The origin of the narrow argentiferous veins is probably related to minor local differential movements of large blocks of diabase or to cooling- contraction of the sheet. More than 500 samples of volcanic rocks were studied by usual palaeomagnetic techniques. The rocks investigated beIong to three different geological periods - the Quaternary - upper Tertiary, the middle Miocene and the lower Cretaceous. The palaeomagnetic data obtained for the individual localities are summarized in the Appendix. Introduction The aim of the paper is to give an outline of palaeomagnetic investigations in Hungary. NEUVONEN and LEO GRUNDSTRÖM Institute of geology, University of Turku, Finland ABSTRACT The dikes of the area can be divided into three groups having different directions of remanent magnetization after demagnetization in the AC field. One of these groups has a direction which coincides with that measured for the Jot- nian dolerites in the Satakunta and Vaasa archipelago. The direction of the second group differs but slightly from this and the third one has a reversed orientation. The age relations and the origin of the magnetization are discussed. According to Sederholm (1890, 1934) the following sequence of dikes can be observed: 1) well preserved olivine diabase (dolerite) on the islands of Market and Sankan in the Aland Sea and near the shore of Eckerö. The rock is the youngest of the intrusive dikes in the region and certainly younger than rapakivi granite because it is found as dikes penetrating it (Fig. 1). 2) coarse grained, plagioclase rich (ossipite) diabase in the region outside the rapakivi gra- nite area. According to Frosterus (1892), these dikes are younger than rapakivi, but Sederholm (1934) and Hausen (1964) consider them to be somewhat older than rapakivi granite and associated granophyric dikes. CONTENTS Introduction 57 Samples 58 Measurements and demagnetization 59 Discussion 61 Introduction Basic dike rocks are abundant and well ex- posed in the region of the Aland (Ahvenanmaa) archipelago. According to Sederholm (1890, 1934) the following sequence of dikes can be observed: 1) well preserved olivine diabase (dolerite) on the islands of Market and Sankan in the Aland Sea and near the shore of Eckerö. The rock is the youngest of the intrusive dikes in the region and certainly younger than rapakivi granite because it is found as dikes penetrating it (Fig. 1). 2) coarse grained, plagioclase rich (ossipite) diabase in the region outside the rapakivi gra- nite area. According to Frosterus (1892), these dikes are younger than rapakivi, but Sederholm (1934) and Hausen (1964) consider them to be somewhat older than rapakivi granite and associated granophyric dikes. The greatest num- ber of these dikes is encontered in an area SE of Föglö and in the SW part of Eckerö (Fig. 1). 8 13902—68 58 K. J. Aleutian Islands is outlined by Coats (1947,1956). Kanaton Ridge (KAN) forms the caldera rim of ancient Mount Kanaton, a broad shield volcano constructed, according to Coats, during late Tertiary and Quaternary time. However, a whole rock K-Ar date run on a sample taken a few feet above the top flow cored gave a date of only 0.18 f0-09 My. The section is composed of a sequence of nearly horizontal basalt and andesite flows, of which eight were sampled. The samples were taken from an eastward trending ridge just outside the ancient caldera rim, and about 45km south-east of Kanaga Volcano (51" 54' N, 182" 54' E). On the basis of pilot AF demagnetization tests (Fig. 2(a), and (b)), the samples were all demagnetized in peak fields of 380Oe. Palaecwecular variation of the geomagnetic field 319 The mean directions from Kanaton are well grouped with the exception of Flow 8 (Fig. 2(c) and (d)). Cores showing magnetically low dips and both normal and reversed directions are present in this flow. It was decided that these cores represent two flows, the one being normal with low dip and high scatter and the other being reversed with low dip but very small scatter (Table 1). This is consistent with relative core locations in the outcrop, though no field evidence for separate flows was noted.

these flows, it is presumed that they were extruded while the geomagnetic field was undergoing a reversal and therefore represent a period of unstable field behaviour (e.g. Creer & Ispir 1970); thus, they have been omitted from the statistical analysis. The remaining seven flows have vector directions and VGP's which are closely grouped (k = 136 and 58, respectively) about the axial dipole field direction and the geographic pole, (Table 1 and Fig. 2(c) and (d)). The distribution is approximately axially symmetric. A clear serial correlation from one flow to the next is evident, indicating that perhaps these seven flows were extruded fairly rapidly and do not represent the full spectrum of secular variation, generally considered to span about lo4 yr, A two-tier analysis (Watson & Irving 1957) was carried out on flows 1-7. Aleutian Islands is outlined by Coats (1947,1956). Kanaton Ridge (KAN) forms the caldera rim of ancient Mount Kanaton, a broad shield volcano constructed, according to Coats, during late Tertiary and Quaternary time. However, a whole rock K-Ar date run on a sample taken a few feet above the top flow cored gave a date of only 0.18 f0-09 My. The section is composed of a sequence of nearly horizontal basalt and andesite flows, of which eight were sampled. The samples were taken from an eastward trending ridge just outside the ancient caldera rim, and about 45km south-east of Kanaga Volcano (51" 54' N, 182" 54' E). On the basis of pilot AF demagnetization tests (Fig. 2(a), and (b)), the samples were all demagnetized in peak fields of 380Oe. Palaecwecular variation of the geomagnetic field 319 The mean directions from Kanaton are well grouped with the exception of Flow 8 (Fig. 2(c) and (d)). Cores showing magnetically low dips and both normal and reversed directions are present in this flow. It was decided that these cores represent two flows, the one being normal with low dip and high scatter and the other being reversed with low dip but very small scatter (Table 1). This is consistent with relative core locations in the outcrop, though no field evidence for separate flows was noted.

these flows, it is presumed that they were extruded while the geomagnetic field was undergoing a reversal and therefore represent a period of unstable field behaviour (e.g. Creer & Ispir 1970); thus, they have been omitted from the statistical analysis. The remaining seven flows have vector directions and VGP's which are closely grouped (k = 136 and 58, respectively) about the axial dipole field direction and the geographic pole, (Table 1 and Fig. 2(c) and (d)). The distribution is approximately axially symmetric. A clear serial correlation from one flow to the next is evident, indicating that perhaps these seven flows were extruded fairly rapidly and do not represent the full spectrum of secular variation, generally considered to span about lo4 yr, A two-tier analysis (Watson & Irving 1957) was carried out on flows 1-7. The variance ratio proved significant at the 95 per cent level so that calculated values for k, and kp are given in Table 2. The number of flows is too small for a reliable measurement of PSV to be possible; nevertheless, we may take kp = 239 as being a minimum measure (maximum k) of PSV during the time of extrusion.
